Eiendom.tekst:
Property companies are among the most natural dividend stocks there are: they own buildings, let them out on long leases, and pass the rental income, less interest and operating costs, on to the owners. The cash flow is the most predictable in the whole catalogue. In return, the sector is the most sensitive to interest rates.

The interest rate sensitivity works through two channels at once, and it is the combination that makes the effect large. The first is the financing cost: property is funded with a lot of debt, and when loans are refinanced at a higher rate, interest eats a larger part of the rental income. The second is the valuation: a property is priced as rental income divided by a required yield, and when interest rates rise, the required yield rises. The value falls even though neither the building nor the tenant has changed.

It pays to keep the two apart when reading a property company's accounts. Changes in property values go through the income statement and can produce huge accounting losses or gains that have nothing to do with the cash flow. A company can report a heavy loss and still fully cover its dividend, because the loss is a write-down and not a cash payment. Rental income less operating costs and interest, not the bottom line, is the figure that decides what can be paid out.

The leases are where the quality of a company lies. The average remaining lease term tells you how long the income is secured, and who the tenants are tells you how secure it is. Public sector tenants and large, solid businesses on ten-year leases give a very different level of safety from many small tenants on short contracts. Most Norwegian office leases are also linked to the consumer price index, so the rent is adjusted for inflation. That is real protection that many other sectors lack.

The segments behave differently. Logistics and warehousing have had a tailwind from the growth of online shopping. Offices depend on employment and on how much space per employee businesses actually need, which working from home has changed. Retail property faces the same pressure from online shopping as the store chains themselves. The sector average therefore says little; it is the make-up of the portfolio that decides.

The loan-to-value ratio is the decisive risk factor for the dividend. Loan terms often require that debt must not exceed a certain share of the property value, and when values fall a company can breach its covenants without anything having gone wrong in the business. The bank then comes first, and the dividend is the first thing to go. A property company with moderate borrowing can withstand a fall in value that forces a highly leveraged company to cut.

Energi.tekst:
The energy sector on Oslo Børs is oil and gas, and the dividend there is driven by three things: the price of what is sold, how much is produced, and how much must be invested to keep production up. The first is outside the companies' control; the other two are decisions they make themselves.

Price sensitivity is the obvious part, but it is not linear. The cost of running a field in production is largely fixed, so the margin between the oil price and the operating cost per barrel is what varies. A company with low production costs keeps a far larger share of a price rise than one with high costs, and survives a price fall that breaks its competitor. Cost per barrel is therefore a more telling figure than production volume.

The Norwegian tax regime is decisive and sets the sector apart from oil companies in other countries. Petroleum activity on the Norwegian continental shelf is taxed with a special tax on top of ordinary corporate tax, so the combined marginal tax rate is very high. In return, investment costs are deductible within the same regime. The effect is that the state carries a large share of both the upside and the downside, and that after-tax cash flow swings less than the oil price would suggest. That damps the dividend in the peak years and supports it in the lean years.

Gas has taken a larger role in revenues than it used to have. Norwegian gas is mainly sold to Europe, and European gas prices have proved able to move quite independently of the oil price, at times far more sharply. For companies weighted towards gas, the European gas price is therefore the relevant indicator, not Brent.

Reserve replacement is the long-term constraint that is rarely discussed in dividend terms. A field runs dry. To keep production up, a company must make new discoveries, buy reserves, or invest in higher recovery from existing fields. All of this costs money that could otherwise have been paid out. A company that pays out a lot and invests little can show a high yield for a few years while production falls away beneath it. The relationship between investment level and production profile says more about how lasting the dividend is than today's payout ratio does.

Several of the companies distinguish between an ordinary dividend they expect to be able to pay through the cycle, and special dividends or buybacks in years with high prices. That split is worth reading up on before using last year's total payout as the basis for a yield calculation. Only one of the two parts is meant to last.

Energitjenester.tekst:
Energy services are the companies that live off the oil companies' investment: seismic, drilling, subsea installation, maintenance, vessels and staffing. They do not sell oil; they sell the work of finding it and getting it out. That makes their dividend depend on something other than the oil price: the oil companies' investment budgets.

The difference matters and is often overlooked. A rising oil price does not immediately bring higher revenue in this sector. It brings higher revenue when the oil companies decide to spend more money, and that decision is taken after the price has stayed high for a while, often a year or two. Conversely, projects already under way carry on for some time after the price has fallen. The sector thus lags the oil price in both directions, which means that a good oil year and a good year for the suppliers are not the same year.

The downturn after 2014 is the formative experience in the sector. The oil price fell from over a hundred dollars to under fifty, the oil companies cut investment hard, and the supplier industry had several years of overcapacity, rate wars and debt restructuring. A number of companies cut their dividend completely. That is why many of the companies in this sector have a shorter unbroken dividend record than their age would suggest. The financial traces of that period are still in the figures.

Day rates are the sector's answer to freight rates. A drilling rig or a construction vessel is hired out by the day, and the gap between a rate that covers the cost of capital and one that only covers operations decides whether the company makes money. As in shipping, supply is slow to adjust: a rig takes years to build, and it cannot be moved into another market if this one fails. Utilisation and contract coverage therefore tell you more about the capacity to pay dividends than revenue does.

Contract length sets the companies apart. A supplier with multi-year framework agreements for maintenance has an income stream that resembles a subscription, while one selling individual jobs in a project market can have a superb year and a dreadful one back to back. Both sit in the same sector table.

The long-term trend is the energy transition. Parts of the expertise in the sector, such as marine operations, foundations, cable laying and underwater work, carry over directly to offshore wind, and several companies have built up renewables businesses alongside their oil services. For the dividend this means two things at once: a new source of demand that does not follow the oil price, and a need for investment that competes with the dividend for the same kroner. Companies in the middle of such a transition often have a lower payout ratio than the accounts alone would suggest.

Finans.tekst:
Finance is by far the largest dividend sector on Oslo Børs, and it is dominated by something foreign investors often misunderstand: the savings banks. A savings bank has no shares in the usual sense. It owns itself, and what it issues to the market is called an equity certificate. The certificate gives a right to a share of the profit and a vote in the board of trustees, but not ownership of the whole bank. The rest of the equity belongs to the bank itself, in what is called the primary capital (ownerless capital that no shareholder owns).

This structure is the whole explanation of why Norwegian savings banks pay so steadily. The profit is split between the equity certificate capital (the certificate holders) and the primary capital in a ratio that is fairly fixed, and the banks have a stated practice of treating the two equally. If a bank cuts the dividend to the certificate holders, it must also hold back from the primary capital, and then the bank stops growing. That builds in a reluctance to cut that you will not find in an ordinary limited company.

The second thing that steers the dividend is capital requirements. The Financial Supervisory Authority of Norway sets minimum requirements for common equity tier one capital, and a bank cannot pay out money it needs to meet them. In practice the banks announce a capital target, and the dividend is whatever is left once the target is met. That is why the payout ratio in the sector often looks high in good years: when the capital is already in place, there is little else to spend the profit on than dividends and buybacks.

The risk is concentrated in two figures. The first is net interest margin, the difference between what the bank charges on loans and pays on deposits. It tends to widen when the policy rate rises quickly, because lending rates are adjusted before deposit rates, and to narrow again when rates fall. Much of the earnings growth in Norwegian banks in recent years comes from here, not from volume growth. The second is loan loss provisions. Norwegian banks have low losses in normal years, but they are heavily exposed to the Norwegian housing market and Norwegian business, and a real downturn in the Norwegian economy hits them at the same time and in the same direction.

For a dividend investor the practical consequence is that the sector offers predictability but little diversification. Owning five savings banks is not the same as owning five independent companies. To a large extent they share the same sensitivity to the economic cycle, the same regulator and the same mortgage book. The diversification lies in which regional markets they serve and how much business lending they have against retail customers, not in reacting differently to an interest rate shock.

Insurance and the other financial companies in the sector partly follow other mechanisms. A property and casualty insurer makes money in two ways: the difference between premiums and claims, and the return on the money that sits waiting to be paid out. The second part means that insurance also likes higher interest rates. The combined ratio, claims and costs as a share of premiums, is the key figure to follow, and a figure below a hundred means that the insurance business on its own runs at a profit.

Forbruksvarer.tekst:
Consumer goods brings together the companies that sell directly to individuals: groceries, branded goods, retail and household services. As a dividend sector it is among the more predictable, for a simple reason: people buy food, clothes and everyday services even in a bad year.

That predictability is unevenly spread, though. There is a big difference between necessities and what can be put off. Grocery retail and everyday products have demand that is almost untouched by the economic cycle, while furniture, electronics and experiences are among the first items a household budget cuts. Two companies in the same sector table can therefore have entirely different resilience. It is not size that decides, but what they sell.

Margins are thin in retail. A grocery chain operates on a few per cent, which makes its profit disproportionately sensitive to small changes in costs. A rise in purchase prices that cannot be passed on to the customer straight away can halve the profit in a quarter. The ability to push through price increases, often called pricing power, is therefore what separates the steady dividend payers from the rest.

Brands have that power to a greater degree than pure distributors. An established brand can adjust its price without losing customers, because the customer buys the brand and not just the product. That is the underlying reason why branded goods companies generally have steadier dividends than retailers, even when they sell into the same market.

Online shopping is the structural pressure. It shifts bargaining power to the consumer by making prices comparable in a few keystrokes, and it lets international players reach Norwegian customers without having shops here. Norwegian consumer companies with large networks of physical stores therefore face both a cost base and a competitive position that have changed for good, not as part of a cycle.

Currency hits this sector in the opposite direction from the export industries. Much of what is sold in Norwegian shops is bought in foreign currency, while revenue is in kroner. A weaker krone thus raises the cost of goods without raising revenue, and the effect comes with a delay of a few months as old purchasing agreements run out. A fall in the krone that is good for shipping stocks is correspondingly bad here.

Fornybar energi.tekst:
Renewable energy is the sector where the dividend is hardest to read from the accounts, because the business model is entirely different from the rest of the catalogue. The companies build power plants that produce for thirty years, and the way that is accounted for fits poorly with a yearly dividend question.

The model is in practice project development. The company finds a site, secures licences, negotiates a long-term power purchase agreement, raises project finance, builds, and is then left with a stake in a plant that brings in income for decades. Much of the debt sits in the individual project rather than with the parent company, and a significant part of the value is stakes in companies that are not fully consolidated. The group accounts therefore give an incomplete picture, and the capacity to pay dividends depends on how much cash can actually be taken up from the projects.

The decisive contract is the power purchase agreement. A plant that has sold its output on a twenty-year agreement at a fixed price has an income stream that resembles a bond: predictable, and little affected by what the power price does. A plant that sells in the spot market is exposed to a price that can swing sharply. The share of contracted output is thus the figure that best tells you how stable the cash flow is.

Interest rates matter unusually much here. A renewables project is a large investment today against income far into the future, and the value of such income falls when rates rise. Higher rates also make project finance more expensive, so that projects that were profitable at low rates no longer are. The period of sharp rate rises from 2022 therefore hit the sector harder than power prices alone would suggest.

The tension between growth and dividends is built in. A company that sees profitable projects ahead has good reason to spend its capital building them rather than paying it out, and investors in the sector have largely bought growth. Dividends have therefore been less common and less stable here than in mature sectors, and a company that starts paying a dividend is often signalling that its pace of growth is slowing.

The political framework is a real risk factor, not just a favourable tailwind. Support schemes, licence terms, grid connection and resource rent taxation decide the profitability of projects that are locked in for decades, and they can be changed by a majority in the Storting, the Norwegian parliament. Companies operating in several countries have spread that risk; those with everything in one market have not.

Havbruk.tekst:
Aquaculture has been among the most profitable industries on Oslo Børs, and its dividend profile follows two things: the salmon price and the biology. The first swings with supply and demand in the world market, the second with what happens in the sea pens.

The price side is simple in principle. Salmon is a commodity with limited supply, because production is regulated through licences and because biology limits how many fish can be kept in the sea. Demand has grown steadily for decades. When supply stalls and demand keeps climbing, the price rises sharply, and because the cost per kilo is fairly fixed in the short term, almost the whole price rise goes to the bottom line. That is the mechanism behind the big profit years.

Biology is the part that sets fish farming apart from other commodity sectors. Sea lice are the chronic cost: treatment costs money, stresses the fish and slows growth, and the lice limits put a ceiling on how many fish a farm can hold. Disease outbreaks can force the culling of a whole site. Algal blooms have on several occasions killed large numbers of fish in a short time. These are losses that cannot be fully insured away, and they hit individual companies in individual regions, not the sector as a whole.

That makes geographical spread a real mark of quality. A company with farms along the whole coast, or with operations in several countries, withstands a local outbreak far better than one with everything in a single fjord. This is one of the few sectors where «where are the farms?» is a relevant question for how safe the dividend is.

The tax side changed substantially in 2023, when the Storting, the Norwegian parliament, introduced a resource rent tax on aquaculture. The reasoning is the same as for hydropower and petroleum: the industry earns an exceptional return from a limited natural resource that the public owns, and part of that return should go to the state. For the dividend investor, the consequence is that after-tax profit in good years is lower than before, and that historical dividends from before the tax cannot simply be used as a template for what the companies can pay out from now on.

The cost side is dominated by feed, which makes up the bulk of the cost per kilo of salmon produced. Feed is based on marine and vegetable raw materials priced internationally, so a rise in commodity markets squeezes margins even when the salmon price is unchanged. The relationship between the salmon price and the feed cost therefore says more about profitability than the salmon price alone.

Taken together, this is a sector that can pay very well, but where individual companies can have a bad year for reasons that have nothing to do with the market. The dividend history should be read with that in mind: a cut can be due to an algal bloom just as easily as to a fall in prices.

Helsevern.tekst:
Health care is a small sector on Oslo Børs, and it is clearly split in two: companies with products on the market that make money, and companies that are developing products and burning capital. Only the first group is relevant as dividend stocks, and the dividing line is sharper here than in any other sector.

What makes established health care companies attractive to a dividend investor is the nature of the demand. The need for medicines, medical equipment and diagnostics follows demographics and the incidence of disease, not the economic cycle. A recession does not reduce the number of patients. Combined with the fact that much of the payment comes from public health budgets rather than from individuals, that gives an income stream that is unusually insensitive to whatever else moves the stock market.

The big risk, on the other hand, is specific and brutal: patent expiry. A drug is protected for a limited number of years, and when the protection lapses, generic competitors come in and the price collapses, often to a fraction within a short time. The income from that product in practice disappears. For a company that depends on one or a few products, this is a known date in the future that the dividend has to be planned around. Breadth in the product portfolio is therefore an important mark of quality.

Regulation is both protection and risk. Approval processes are long and expensive, which keeps competitors out and protects the margins of whoever gets through first. At the same time an authority can change reimbursement schemes or push prices down, and in countries with publicly funded health care, such as Norway, the single customer is also the one that sets the price. Price pressure from the public sector is a lasting factor, not a one-off event.

Equipment and consumables companies have a different profile from drug makers, and for the dividend often a better one. They sell instruments that are used for years and consumables that must be bought again and again, and they face no patent cliff in the same way. Recurring sales of consumables to an installed base are one of the most stable forms of income there is.

Research spending is the item that competes with the dividend. A health care company that stops developing new products can raise its dividend for a few years, but undermines its income further ahead. The ratio of research spending to revenue therefore says something about how lasting the dividend is: a strikingly low level can be a sign that the dividend is being funded by the future.

Industri.tekst:
Industrials is the broadest sector in the catalogue, which makes it hard to sum up. It covers everything from contractors that build roads and housing, through engineering and defence suppliers, to pure technology companies that are classed as industrials because they supply equipment. The dividend profiles vary just as widely.

The common thread is nonetheless the order book. An industrial company rarely sells off the shelf; it wins contracts that are delivered over months or years. That gives a very different visibility from the commodity sectors: when order intake falls, management knows long before it shows up in the results, and can adjust the dividend in time. Conversely, a weak quarter is rarely enough to threaten the dividend, as long as the order backlog holds.

That is why order intake and order backlog are the figures that say most about the dividend ahead, more than the quarter's revenue. A backlog that covers more than a year of production is a very different starting point from one that covers a quarter.

Margins are the second key point, and they are tighter than many assume. Contracting runs on a margin of a few per cent, and a fixed-price contract that goes wrong can wipe out the profit from several that went well. This is a sector where single projects can overturn a year's result. Companies with many small contracts therefore have steadier dividends than companies with a few large ones, regardless of how profitable they are on average.

The cost side is dominated by wages, steel and energy. Norwegian industrial companies compete with low-cost countries on price and with the rest of the Nordic region on expertise, and a weak krone helps those that export while it punishes those that buy inputs abroad. It is worth checking which of the two a company actually is, because the exchange rate pulls in opposite directions for the two groups.

Sensitivity to the economic cycle varies more than the sector name suggests. Companies that supply the public sector, such as transport, defence and infrastructure, have demand that follows government budgets more than the cycle, and they have kept their dividends through downturns in which the construction industry cut. Companies that supply the housing market or private business investment swing far more. Two industrial stocks can therefore carry entirely different dividend risk even though they sit in the same table.

For the dividend investor, this breadth means that the sector average is of little use as a guide. A yield above the average means nothing until you know whether the company is a contractor in a cyclical market or a supplier on long-term public contracts. There is more to gain here from reading the individual company than from comparing within the sector.

Informasjonsteknologi.tekst:
The IT sector on Oslo Børs bears little resemblance to the American one. The platform companies with huge margins are not here; what is listed is mainly consultancies, systems integrators and niche software suppliers. That gives a dividend profile that is far more stable, and far less spectacular, than the sector name suggests.

The consultancy model is easy to understand and explains most of it. Revenue is the number of consultants, times the share of their time that is billed, times the hourly rate. It is a business with little capital tied up: there is no factory, no fleet and no warehouse. The profit therefore largely becomes free cash flow, and because there is little to invest in, much of it can be paid out. That is the main reason several companies in the sector have long, steady dividend records.

The key figure is the billing rate. Costs, which in practice means wages, run whether the consultants have work or not, so a fall of a few percentage points in utilisation hits the margin hard. This is also where a downturn shows up first: businesses that need to cut tend to cut their use of consultants before they lay off their own staff. The sector is thus less cyclical than energy and shipping, but it is not insensitive, and it feels a downturn early.

The competition for people is a lasting cost driver. A consultancy's only real resource is employees who can leave for a competitor, and in periods when developers are scarce, wages are pushed up faster than hourly rates can be adjusted. The margin can then fall in a year in which revenue grows nicely.

The public sector is an unusually important customer in Norway. The state, municipalities and health trusts buy IT services on a large scale, and they do so through long framework agreements. A supplier with a heavy public sector portfolio therefore has more predictable income than one selling to private business, and that has shown in the stability of its dividend through several downturns.

The software companies in the sector follow a different logic. The shift from selling licences to selling subscriptions gives steadier income over time, but it costs money during the transition: revenue is spread over the subscription period instead of being booked at the sale. A company in the middle of such a change can look weaker than it is, and a dividend held flat through such a phase is often a better sign than it appears.

What to follow over time are the shifts in technology. A systems integrator lives off complexity at its customers, and tools that reduce that complexity are both an opportunity and a threat. The sector has lower cyclical risk and higher structural risk than average. The dividend is seldom threatened by the economic cycle, but more often by the business model changing beneath the company.

Kommunikasjonstjenester.tekst:
Communication services covers media and online marketplace companies: those that make money from attention and from connecting buyers and sellers. The dividend here is closely tied to the advertising market, and the advertising market is one of the most cyclical items there is in a company budget.

The reason is that marketing is easy to cut and easy to switch back on. When a business needs to save quickly, the advertising budget is among the first to be reduced, because the effect of the cut is not felt in the short term. That means media groups' revenue falls earlier and more steeply in a downturn than the rest of the economy, and picks up just as quickly when it turns.

Digital marketplaces are a far better business model than traditional advertising, and the two are worth telling apart. A marketplace with an established position in property, cars or jobs has a network effect: the sellers are there because the buyers are there, and the other way round. That gives a position that is hard to attack and a pricing power that lets revenue grow without a matching growth in costs. Several of the most stable dividend payers in this sector are marketplaces, not media.

The structural challenge for traditional media is well known, but worth spelling out: advertising money has moved to global platforms that can target better and sell more cheaply. What remains of print and linear revenue falls year by year, and the question for the dividend is whether digital subscriptions grow faster than the old revenue disappears. The transition has worked for some and not for others, and the dividend history separates the two groups quite clearly.

Subscription revenue is therefore the mark of quality to look for. It is recurring, it is not very sensitive to the cycle compared with advertising, and it makes the cash flow predictable. A company where subscriptions make up a growing share of revenue has a very different dividend risk from one that still depends on the advertising market, whatever today's yield suggests.

The cost side is dominated by content and technology, and both are largely fixed. That gives considerable operating leverage: a small fall in revenue hits the result hard, and a small rise does the same in the other direction. It explains why the dividend in this sector can move more than the revenue figures alone would suggest.

AKRBP.tekst:
Aker BP was built through acquisitions. The company was called Det norske oljeselskap until 2016, when it bought BP's Norwegian business and BP became a co-owner. In 2022 the oil and gas business of Sweden's Lundin Energy was added. Aker ASA is the largest owner and BP the second largest, and the head office is at Fornebu. All production is on the Norwegian continental shelf. Aker BP is operator of the Alvheim, Eiga (Edvard Grieg and Ivar Aasen), Skarv, Ula and Valhall field hubs, and is a partner in Johan Sverdrup, where Equinor is operator. The company therefore controls the costs and the schedule for most of its portfolio itself. In return, its income is concentrated on one shelf and under one tax regime, and oil and gas are sold in dollars.

Up to 2027 the company is in a period of heavy investment. Yggdrasil, a new development Aker BP operates in the area between Oseberg and Alvheim, is planned to start in 2027 together with Valhall PWP-Fenris and the third phase of Johan Sverdrup. The cost estimate for Valhall PWP-Fenris was raised in February 2026, partly because the well programme was expanded. Until the projects produce, a large part of the cash flow goes to construction, and the income from them comes only later.

The dividend is declared in dollars. The board sets an amount per quarter at the start of the year and keeps it fixed through the year, and for 2026 it was raised at the turn of the year. The company describes it as a dividend meant to withstand swings in the oil price, and it is in years with large investments and lower prices that this promise is tested. For a Norwegian shareholder the krone amount varies with the dollar exchange rate.

DNB.tekst:
DNB is Norway's largest financial group, with roots that go back to Christiania Sparebank, a savings bank founded in 1822. Today's bank was built through large mergers. Bergen Bank and Den norske Creditbank became Den norske Bank in 1990, and the merger with Gjensidige NOR in 2003 created DnB NOR. The name DNB came in 2011. The state is the largest owner through the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries, and Sparebankstiftelsen DNB, a savings bank foundation, is the second largest.

Most of the income is interest, the difference between what the bank charges on loans and what it pays on deposits. Lending is heavily weighted towards Norwegian home mortgages, while corporate customers account for more of the risk of losses. Outside Norway, DNB has specialised in ocean industries and energy, financing ships, offshore and power. Postbanken and Sbanken are also brands within the group. In March 2025 DNB bought the Swedish investment bank Carnegie, and the business now operates as DNB Carnegie. That makes fees from advisory work, share trading and asset management a larger part of income than before.

How much can be paid out is set by capital requirements. A bank must hold a certain amount of equity relative to its lending, and only what lies above the requirement and the bank's own buffer is free. DNB aims to pay out more than half of its profit as a cash dividend and to raise the dividend per share in kroner from year to year. Capital beyond that goes to buybacks of its own shares or extra dividends. Carnegie was paid for in cash, and acquisitions of this kind draw on the same capital.

EQNR.tekst:
Equinor was founded by the Norwegian state as Statoil in 1972. In 1981 it became the first Norwegian company to be made operator of a field, Gullfaks. The company was listed in 2001, merged with Norsk Hydro's oil and gas business in 2007 and took the name Equinor in 2018. The state is the largest owner through the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries, and a parliamentary resolution from 2001 says the state shall own at least two thirds of the company.

The Norwegian continental shelf is the backbone of the business, and under the strategy presented at the 2026 capital markets day it is to receive most of the investment up to 2030. From there Equinor sells oil, pipeline gas and LNG, mostly to Europe. Outside Norway it produces oil and gas in the United States, Brazil, Angola, the United Kingdom and Canada, among other countries. On top of that comes a power business with offshore wind and other generation that is still small next to oil and gas, and a trading arm that buys and sells oil, gas and power.

The cash dividend is declared quarterly in US dollars. The krone amount is converted at Norges Bank's dollar rate around the record date, so a Norwegian shareholder can receive a different amount in kroner from one quarter to the next even when the dollar dividend is unchanged. The aim is to raise the quarterly dividend per share every year. The rest of what the company wants to return goes to share buybacks, and their size follows oil and gas prices and the strength of the balance sheet. The state takes part in the buybacks through the redemption of a proportional share of its own shares, so that its stake stays the same. Shares that are bought back are cancelled, which means later dividends are shared among fewer shares.

FRO.tekst:
Frontline owns tankers for crude oil and oil products in three sizes, from the huge VLCCs down to LR2/Aframax. The company is registered in Cyprus, but day-to-day operations are run from Oslo by Frontline Management AS. Its legal domicile was moved from Bermuda to Cyprus in December 2022. The share trades in both Oslo and New York, and the largest shareholder is Hemen Holding, which is owned through trusts John Fredriksen has set up for his family.

Most of the fleet trades in the spot market, where income follows the day rate voyage by voyage. In periods of high rates Frontline locks in part of its income by chartering out ships on time charter. It did this with one-year contracts for several VLCCs in January 2026, and with two- and three-year contracts the following summer. At the same time the fleet is being renewed. Early in 2026 Frontline sold several of its oldest VLCCs and bought newbuilding contracts for modern ships with scrubbers from a company associated with Hemen. The purchase is financed with cash and new loans, and the gain from selling the old ships is a one-off item.

The aim is a quarterly dividend equal or close to adjusted earnings per share. The dividend therefore mirrors the freight market almost directly and can swing sharply from one quarter to the next. Gains from sales can also go straight back to shareholders: after the sale of two VLCCs in the autumn of 2026, a one-off dividend came on top of the quarterly dividend. The dividend is set in dollars. Loans finance a large part of the fleet, and interest and instalments come before the payout. In 2026 the company negotiated down the interest margin on several of its loans.

GJF.tekst:
Gjensidige was set up as a customer-owned insurance company, and that still shapes its ownership. The largest owner is the Gjensidige Foundation (Gjensidigestiftelsen), which under its articles passes the dividend tied to the year's result on to the non-life insurance customers in Norway. Norwegian customers have received such a customer dividend every year since the listing in 2010. For an ordinary shareholder, this means that most of the regular dividend goes to an owner that passes the money on, and that aims to own well over half of the shares over time. The arrangement is also part of the business model, because the customer dividend gives customers a reason to stay.

Income comes mainly from non-life insurance for individuals, businesses, agriculture and the public sector in Norway and Denmark. In Sweden Gjensidige is smaller and challenges the established companies. Motor, home, travel and personal insurance are the largest products. The business in the Baltics was sold to ERGO, and the sale was completed in January 2026. Alongside insurance, a subsidiary offers defined contribution pensions and savings in Norway, and Gjensidige Mobility Group owns the vehicle recovery company REDGO and Flyt, which administers toll collection.

The dividend policy has two parts. The regular dividend shall grow over time and make up at least four fifths of profit after tax. If capital is larger than the company needs, the excess is paid out on top as a special dividend, as was done for the 2025 financial year. How much counts as excess is decided by the solvency requirements for insurance companies, and that time the Financial Supervisory Authority of Norway had to approve the payout before the general meeting voted on it. The result has two sources: the insurance operations, where claims and costs are meant to be lower than premiums, and the return on the money the company has invested.

KOG.tekst:
Kongsberg Gruppen became a pure defence and technology company in April 2026. Kongsberg Maritime was then spun off and admitted to trading as a separate company, and shareholders received one share in the new company for each share they held. What remains is two business areas. Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace makes the Naval Strike Missile (NSM), the Joint Strike Missile for the F-35, the NASAMS air defence system and remote weapon stations, and its customers are Norway, NATO countries and other allies. Kongsberg Discovery makes echo sounders, sonars and other underwater technology for seabed mapping, fisheries and ocean research, and also supplies navies. The group also owns almost half of the Finnish defence company Patria and half of the satellite company KSAT.

Its roots go back to Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk, founded in 1814, and the company was listed in 1993. The state, through the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries, kept a majority of the shares at the listing and is still the largest owner.

The dividend policy is set in kroner per share, not as a share of profit. The aim is an ordinary dividend that holds steady or rises from year to year. When capital allows, additional dividends and buybacks of its own shares come on top, and for the 2025 financial year the additional dividend was larger than the ordinary one. The total can therefore swing more than the ordinary dividend does. What limits the room is investment. Demand for missiles and air defence has required large expansions of production: the group is building missile factories in Australia and the United States and has bought the American missile company Zone 5. The board itself writes that all distributions are weighed against future capital needs. The company has paid a dividend every year since the listing, except in 2000 and 2001.

MOWI.tekst:
Mowi is the world's largest producer of Atlantic salmon and runs fish farming in Norway, Scotland, Ireland, the Faroe Islands, Iceland, Canada and Chile. The Icelandic part is Arctic Fish in the Westfjords, where Mowi owns the majority and which has its own share listing on Euronext Growth Oslo. The name goes back to Mowi, the fish farming company the Mowinckel family started in the 1960s. The group was long called Marine Harvest and took the old name back from 1 January 2019.

What sets Mowi apart from the other salmon stocks is how much of the chain it owns itself. Mowi Feed has two feed plants, one in Norway and one in Scotland. After a strategic review, the board decided in December 2025 to keep them and instead make the feed to Skretting's recipes, cooperating on purchasing and logistics. At the other end of the chain the group has value-added processing in Europe, the United States and Asia and sells smoked salmon, portions and ready meals, partly under the MOWI brand. In Northern Norway Mowi has grown through the purchase of Nova Sea in 2025 and an agreement from March 2026 to take over the sea farming business of Torghatten Aqua.

The dividend goes ex four times a year. The policy is that the ordinary quarterly dividend shall under normal conditions be at least half of underlying earnings per share, and that capital the company does not need shall be paid out as an extraordinary dividend. The amount therefore follows earnings from quarter to quarter, and a weak quarter quickly shows up in the next payout. The group reports in euros, while the dividend is declared in Norwegian kroner, so the krone exchange rate also affects what is left for shareholders.

NHY.tekst:
Norsk Hydro was founded in 1905 by Sam Eyde and Kristian Birkeland, and the fertiliser business was spun off as Yara in 2004. What remains is an aluminium group that owns the chain from mine to finished profile. The bauxite is mined at Paragominas in the Brazilian state of Pará and refined into alumina at Alunorte, which Hydro itself describes as the world's largest alumina refinery outside China. Both were bought from the mining company Vale in 2011, together with the majority in the Albras smelter next door. Alumina is turned into metal at the plants in Norway and at Qatalum in Qatar, which Hydro half owns, among other places. At the far end of the chain Hydro makes profiles for buildings, cars and industry and remelts used aluminium.

Power and gas are the heavy costs. The Norwegian plants run on hydropower, partly from Hydro's own power stations and partly on long-term contracts. In 2025 Hydro secured power for Sunndal and Høyanger for the years 2031 to 2040 through two agreements with Hafslund, and the company is investing in the Illvatn pumped storage plant. Outside Norway, gas is the weak point. When gas deliveries in Qatar were cut in March 2026, Qatalum had to cut production sharply, and from August the same year Alunorte did not receive the gas its contract promised and had to buy at spot prices.

Under the dividend policy at least half of adjusted net income is to go to the ordinary dividend, measured over a full cycle, and a fixed minimum amount per share is the floor. In strong years buybacks or extra dividends come on top. Earnings follow the aluminium price on the London Metal Exchange, the alumina price and the krone exchange rate, so the dividend swings a great deal from year to year, while the floor limits how far it can fall. The state is the largest owner.

TEL.tekst:
Telenor was founded as Telegrafverket in 1855, was called Televerket from 1969 and took the name Telenor in 1995. The company was listed on Oslo Børs in December 2000, and the state is still the largest owner through the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries. In Norway, Telenor is the largest player in both mobile and broadband. The company describes itself as the only telecom operator with significant operations in all four Nordic countries, with Telenor in Norway, Sweden and Denmark and DNA in Finland. In July 2026 Telenor agreed to buy a controlling stake in the Swedish broadband provider Bahnhof.

The Asian business has shrunk quickly. Telenor Pakistan was sold at the turn of 2025/2026, and in January 2026 Telenor agreed to sell its stake in Thailand's True Corporation. What remains is the majority in Grameenphone in Bangladesh and a minority stake in CelcomDigi in Malaysia. The past in the region still follows the company: in September 2026 Telenor ASA was charged in a case about its former business in Myanmar.

The dividend for a financial year is declared as one amount and split in two, with one part paid in June and one in October. The policy is that the ordinary dividend per share shall rise from year to year, and in recent years the increases have been small. Telenor also buys back its own shares. In the programme from May 2026 a proportional share of the state's shares is redeemed, so that the state's stake stays the same, and the shares are cancelled afterwards. The company itself calls 2026 a transition year, with parallel IT systems and restructuring costs that are planned to decline towards the end of the year and through 2027.

VAR.tekst:
Vår Energi traces its roots back to the first production licence on the Norwegian continental shelf in 1965, through what was long called Eni Norge. Today's company was formed in 2018, when Eni Norge merged with Point Resources. Since then it has grown through acquisitions: ExxonMobil's stakes in fields operated by others came in 2019, and Neptune Energy's Norwegian business in 2024. Vår Energi was listed in February 2022, and Italy's Eni is still the largest owner with a clear majority of the shares.

The company holds stakes in many of the producing fields on the Norwegian shelf. It is itself operator of Balder, Ringhorne, Gjøa and Duva in the North Sea, Fenja in the Norwegian Sea and Goliat in the Barents Sea. A large part of the gas is sold to Europe. This breadth means a production stop at one field matters less for the whole than at a producer with few fields, but everything still lies on one shelf and under one tax regime.

The dividend is set as a total dollar amount for the whole company each quarter. It is converted to kroner per share at Norges Bank's dollar rate when the dividend is announced. The long-term policy ties the payout to a share of cash flow from operations after tax, viewed over a full cycle. In July 2026 Vår Energi and BlueNord agreed to merge, and BlueNord's shareholders are to receive new shares in Vår Energi and cash. This gives Vår Energi production outside Norway for the first time, from Tyra and the other hubs in the Danish North Sea. The company has said the merger will increase its capacity to pay out, but the dividend will also be shared among more shares than before.
